---
title: "Fictional Army - Filtering and Sorting - Solutions"
output: html_document
---

### Introduction:

This exercise was inspired by this [page](http://chrisalbon.com/python/)

Special thanks to: https://github.com/chrisalbon for sharing the dataset and materials.

In R, the closest thing to the pandas index is the **row names** of a base `data.frame`
(tibbles do not keep row names). In this exercise we use row names together with
`[rows, columns]` indexing, which works like `.loc` (with names) and `.iloc` (with positions).
Remember that R counts positions from 1, not from 0.

### Step 1. Import the necessary libraries

```{r step1, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
```

### Step 2. This is the data given as a list

```{r given-data}
# Create an example dataset about a fictional army
raw_data <- list(
  regiment = c("Nighthawks", "Nighthawks", "Nighthawks", "Nighthawks", "Dragoons", "Dragoons", "Dragoons", "Dragoons", "Scouts", "Scouts", "Scouts", "Scouts"),
  company = c("1st", "1st", "2nd", "2nd", "1st", "1st", "2nd", "2nd", "1st", "1st", "2nd", "2nd"),
  deaths = c(523, 52, 25, 616, 43, 234, 523, 62, 62, 73, 37, 35),
  battles = c(5, 42, 2, 2, 4, 7, 8, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9),
  size = c(1045, 957, 1099, 1400, 1592, 1006, 987, 849, 973, 1005, 1099, 1523),
  veterans = c(1, 5, 62, 26, 73, 37, 949, 48, 48, 435, 63, 345),
  readiness = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3),
  armored = c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1),
  deserters = c(4, 24, 31, 2, 3, 4, 24, 31, 2, 3, 2, 3),
  origin = c("Arizona", "California", "Texas", "Florida", "Maine", "Iowa", "Alaska", "Washington", "Oregon", "Wyoming", "Louisana", "Georgia")
)
```

### Step 3. Create a dataframe and assign it to a variable called army.

#### Don't forget to keep the columns in the order presented in the list ('regiment', 'company', 'deaths'...) so that the column order is consistent with the solutions.

```{r}
army <- as.data.frame(raw_data)
army
```

### Step 4. Set the 'origin' colum as the index (row names) of the dataframe

```{r}
army <- column_to_rownames(army, "origin")
army
```

### Step 5. Print only the column veterans

```{r}
army$veterans

# keeping the row names
army["veterans"]
```

### Step 6. Print the columns 'veterans' and 'deaths'

```{r}
army[, c("veterans", "deaths")]
```

### Step 7. Print the name of all the columns.

```{r}
names(army)
```

### Step 8. Select the 'deaths', 'size' and 'deserters' columns from Maine and Alaska

```{r}
army[c("Maine", "Alaska"), c("deaths", "size", "deserters")]
```

### Step 9. Select the rows 3 to 7 and the columns 3 to 6

```{r}
army[3:7, 3:6]
```

### Step 10. Select every row after the fourth row and all columns

```{r}
army[5:nrow(army), ]
```

### Step 11. Select every row up to the 4th row and all columns

```{r}
army[1:4, ]
```

### Step 12. Select the 3rd column up to the 7th column

```{r}
army[, 3:7]
```

### Step 13. Select rows where df.deaths is greater than 50

```{r}
army[army$deaths > 50, ]

# the dplyr way
army |> filter(deaths > 50)
```

### Step 14. Select rows where df.deaths is greater than 500 or less than 50

```{r}
army |> filter(deaths > 500 | deaths < 50)
```

### Step 15. Select all the regiments not named "Dragoons"

```{r}
army |> filter(regiment != "Dragoons")
```

### Step 16. Select the rows called Texas and Arizona

```{r}
army[c("Texas", "Arizona"), ]
```

### Step 17. Select the third cell in the row named Arizona

```{r}
army["Arizona", 3]
```

### Step 18. Select the third cell down in the column named deaths

```{r}
army[3, "deaths"]
```
